To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise flexible working to reflect carers and diverse personal circumstances. Expanding part-time roles, job-sharing, and phased retirement, together with strong childcare support and accessible mental health services for staff, will help reduce burnout and widen the pool of people able to work in primary care. 

Equally important is expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams. Nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied professionals should have clear training, supervision and defined scopes of practice so they can share routine GP workloads safely. This needs robust CPD, dependable supervision, and practical rostering that covers gaps without leaving teams overstretched. 

Local co-location and digital tools can support this by enabling triage and signposting to flow smoothly between primary, community and specialist care. In my experience, practices that combine flexible staffing with well-supported MDTs retain staff longer, reduce burnout, and keep appointment access consistent while preserving safety and patient choice.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise people and systems together: invest in interoperable IT that lets primary care, community services and mental health teams share up-to-date information quickly and safely, so clinicians can see the full picture and act fast. Strong, secure data systems are essential; staff need reliable tools, regular cyber security training, and clear governance so patient safety isn’t compromised. Equally important is investing in staff development—comprehensive, ongoing digital training, protected time for learning new tools, and digital champions in every team to support peers.

Crucially, we must safeguard non-digital routes for those who are digitally excluded: maintain ample phone and in-person booking channels, and provide local digital access and literacy support so people aren’t left behind. Multilingual information and interpreters should be integrated with digital systems to avoid widening gaps.

A sustainable plan should also expand multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics) to share workload and maintain safety, with realistic rosters and robust supervision to prevent burnout. Practical examples, like pharmacist-led reviews reducing GP waits and improving satisfaction, show what works and should be scaled up while digital tools are rolled out.

Prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, robust modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring; use these to target recruitment, retention and training while safeguarding safe, high-quality care and avoiding overreliance on digital-only solutions.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Local dashboards on staffing levels, skill mix, vacancies, turnover and caseloads must be shared with trusts and commissioners to drive timely action. This should be paired with scenario modelling to forecast demand and test the impact of longer appointment times and embedded teams. Crucially, safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models must be at the core. Where patients benefit from a named clinician or a stable care team, we need sufficient staffing to sustain those relationships, be it GPs, district nurses, or mental health staff. Real-time safety monitoring and escalation pathways should accompany access improvements, with thresholds to pause or adjust if quality metrics dip. Examples: ensure same-day slots are staffed with adequate nursing and admin support; monitor indicators such as unplanned admissions after primary care contact, appointment adherence, and patient experience. Invest in training, career progression and wellbeing to reduce burnout. This approach would help protect care quality while expanding timely access.

An NHS workforce plan should first secure funded career pathways that reward experience and enable progression from entry roles to advanced practice, with protected CPD time and structured mentorship. Return-to-practice schemes must be simple and well-supported so experienced clinicians can re-enter safely after a break. Evidence from local trusts shows mentorship accelerates onboarding and improves morale; protected CPD reduces turnover. Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams to share GP workload more safely. Invest in nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and AHPs with standardised training, supervision and clear scopes of practice. This should be backed by integrated supervision models and digital decision-support to avoid delay and errors. With proper redistribution, GPs can focus on complex cases while team members manage triage, routine reviews and care navigation, improving timely access and safety. Third, pilot and scale workforce models with robust data. Local dashboards should guide recruitment, retention, and rostering; flexible, well-paid contracts and targeted recruitment to underserved areas. All measures must be funded against safe, high-quality care benchmarks and linked to patient outcomes.

Prioritise a stable, long-term funding framework to grow training and capacity, plus responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, credential recognition, and strong integration safeguards to protect source health systems; balance with strong retention, wellbeing, and flexible staffing to keep high-quality care.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, sustainable staffing and manageable workloads so clinicians can keep delivering high‑quality care. That means predictable rosters, protected time for training and supervision, and clear career pathways to attract and retain staff across general practice, mental health and community teams. Flexible working, strong wellbeing support, and practical steps to reduce administrative burden are essential, as is targeted support and incentives for roles in hard‑to‑staff areas. 

Equally important is investment in interoperable IT and secure systems that enable seamless information sharing between GP practices, hospitals and mental health services. Staff must receive ongoing digital training to use telemedicine, remote monitoring and digital triage confidently, with robust cyber security. Importantly, the plan must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients: maintain telephone access, in‑person clinics, paper forms and staff who can help people build digital confidence in the community. 

From personal experience, continuity of care and IT that actually supports clinicians—not creates extra work—leads to better outcomes and less downstream demand. A phased rollout with pilots in different settings, properly funded and evaluated, will help us recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality.

Prioritise secure, multi-year ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce initiatives and expand training capacity, reduce short-term policy volatility, plus investment in interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training—while safeguarding alternatives for those digitally excluded, to recruit, retain, and support safe care.

I firmly support a NHS workforce plan that expands and regulates multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload while maintaining high-quality care. Our GP practices are under real pressure, and increasingly the right mix of skills—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals—can handle a broader range of need without compromising safety. The plan should fund and govern these teams so every member operates within clear, evidence-based scopes and under robust supervision.

Key priorities I’d like to see:
- Clear scope, governance and supervision for all MDT members
  - Define what tasks each role can undertake, with formal supervision arrangements and escalation paths to GPs or specialists when needed.
  - Establish competency frameworks and regular reassessment to ensure patient safety and care consistency.
- Structured training and career development
  - Create unified training pipelines so staff move from foundational to advanced practices (e.g., pharmacist-led medicines optimisation, nurse-led chronic disease management, PA-led clinics) with recognised qualifications.
  - Provide protected time for ongoing learning, mentorship, and leadership development to improve retention and job satisfaction.
- Safe redistribution of GP workload
  - Use MDTs to handle triage, routine follow-ups, chronic disease management and minor illnesses, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases and urgent concerns.
  - Give practices the option of extended hours or dedicated MDT-led clinics to improve access without sacrificing care quality.
- Adequate staffing and equitable distribution
  - Plan staffing needs locally, with flexible pools of nurses, pharmacists, PAs and paramedics to cover peak times and deprived areas where access gaps are sharp.
  - Include robust backfill arrangements and guaranteed supervision to prevent burnout and maintain continuity.
- Integrated systems and data sharing
  - Invest in interoperable IT so MDT members can access and contribute to single care plans, reducing handover errors and duplication of work.
  - Implement real-time safety and quality dashboards to monitor outcomes, wait times and escalation rates.
- Quality assurance and patient safety culture
  - Require regular clinical audits and peer review within MDTs, ensuring parity of care and rapid learning from near-misses or adverse events.
  - Maintain patient-informed consent and choice, with clear explanations of who is providing care and why.
- Community-facing approaches to recruitment and retention
  - Pair workforce planning with local recruitment campaigns, supportive work environments, sufficient supervision, and opportunities for progression in community settings to improve retention.

In practice, I’ve seen how well-embedded multidisciplinary teams can work. In one local practice, pharmacists joined the MDT to review complex medication regimens for older patients. This not only improved safety around polypharmacy but also freed up GP time to deal with more urgent issues. In another example, a physician associate-led clinic helped with follow-ups for chronic conditions, reducing unnecessary GP visits and shortening waiting times for patients with stable conditions. Paramedics and nurse practitioners have piloted home visit pathways for high-need patients, which cut hospital avoidable contacts and supported better patient experience.

All of this must be underpinned by credible funding and governance. The plan should ensure that MDT expansion is not merely a cost saving exercise, but a step toward safer, more accessible care that retains staff by offering meaningful career paths, strong supervision, and a culture of continuous improvement. The goal is to keep high-quality care accessible to everyone, particularly in communities most at risk of being left behind, while easing the unsustainable burden on already stretched GPs.

If implemented with clear standards, adequate resources, and a real focus on supervision and patient safety, expanding multidisciplinary teams can help deliver timely, appropriate care without compromising quality—and that aligns with my experience and the needs I’ve heard about in our area.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding the education pipeline—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places—with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships. I’m not naïve enough to think simply piling in more students will fix everything; what matters is tying those training opportunities to real, well-supported service delivery so trainees become capable, confident clinicians who stay in the system. In my view, the aim should be to grow the domestic primary care supply while safeguarding the quality and safety of care people rely on today.

First, protect and structure training in a way that preserves continuity of care for patients. In practice, that means trainees should have stable supervision, clearly defined competencies, and real access to ongoing patient relationships rather than being shuffled through rotating placements with limited real responsibility. The experience I’ve had with practices where new patients were redirected to a rotating GP during absences showed how quickly care becomes fragmented and how much history needs to be re-explained at every visit. Protected placements with consistent supervisors and longer-term attachments to teams would help avoid that problem and accelerate learning in a way that benefits patients too.

Second, ensure the training expansion translates into safer, higher-quality care from day one. This requires robust mentoring, adequate support staff in each practice (nurses, pharmacists, care coordinators, admin help), and realistic caseloads so trainees aren’t overwhelmed. It also means practical, well-supervised return-to-practice pathways for experienced clinicians who have paused or reduced their hours. If we want more domestic supply, we must make the working environment sustainable now, not just promise a pipeline for the future.

Third, align education with workforce needs in the community and mental health settings. Our area has urgent gaps in timely access to talking therapies and community teams. A plan that expands training but doesn’t prioritise immediate recruitment into these teams risks a bigger flood of new graduates into general practice without the necessary back-up in mental health and social care. Protected placements should be paired with clear routes into community health and psychological supports so new clinicians gain a full picture of patient journeys and not just pocketed clinical tasks.

Fourth, recognise the importance of retention and workload management. Incentives to stay, flexible rostering, and the right mix of clinical and support roles are essential if newly trained staff are to remain in post. In parallel, we need to protect the pensions and employment terms that older, more experienced clinicians rely on, alongside smart workforce planning that distributes staff fairly between rural and urban areas. A successful plan will balance growing capacity with preserving the personal, long-term relationships that many patients depend on.

Fifth, ensure access and equity aren’t sacrificed in the rush to train more. Digital systems have their place, but we must avoid leaving older patients or those without reliable internet behind. Training pipelines should include competencies in delivering high-quality care through multiple channels—face-to-face, telephone, and where possible, protected in-person clinics for patients who need them most.

In short, I’d like to see a workforce plan that simultaneously expands the pipeline and strengthens the fabric of day-to-day care: protected, high-quality training placements; firm supervision and mentoring; better staffing at the practice level; clear return-to-practice routes; and a strong emphasis on retaining experienced staff and supporting community and mental health services. If the policy focuses only on numbers or a one-size-fits-all expansion, we’ll end up with more graduates who still can’t access the continuity and predictability that patients, particularly the elderly with chronic conditions, rely on. That would be a missed opportunity. We must build a sustainable, patient-centered workforce that delivers safe, high-quality care today and tomorrow.

From my perspective living in England and watching GP, community and mental health teams feel the squeeze, the most important thing for an NHS workforce plan is that it is data-driven, locally tailored and openly reviewed. We need a clear framework that shows what we have, what we need and how we’ll measure progress. A core priority should be to develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Without that, we’re guessing, and funding can drift away from what actually makes a difference on the ground.

- Transparent local data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks
  - Build local intelligence on vacancies, sickness, turnover, skill mix and workload, not just national averages. Publish these in accessible formats for staff and patients so decisions are visible and accountable.
  - Use forward-looking modelling to forecast demand, training needs and retirement attrition, with scenarios that test different funding levels and workforce configurations.
  - Establish clear evaluation frameworks that link funding to outcomes: wait times, continuity of care, safety indicators, MDT productivity, patient satisfaction and avoidable admissions. If it isn’t measuring something meaningful, we shouldn’t assume it’s working.
  - In practice, where our area has tested local dashboards and quarterly reviews, managers can spot bottlenecks early and reallocate support before a crisis emerges. It makes planning less reactive and more strategic.

- Sustainable recruitment and retention that recognises local realities
  - Targeted recruitment campaigns and practical return-to-practice routes, with robust credentialing and settlement support so new staff can contribute quickly and feel valued.
  - Improve pay, pensions and career progression for GPs, nurses and allied health staff, plus reliable locum cover to avoid unsafe overloads. Flexible working patterns and predictable rosters help retain staff who might otherwise leave.
  - Prioritise wellbeing and mental health supports for staff, easy access to occupational health, and a culture where asking for help is normal. In places where wellbeing is treated as a core objective, turnover and sickness absence fall and patient care improves.

- Multidisciplinary teams that genuinely share care and records
  - Expand MDTs in primary care and community hubs to include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates who can manage routine work and triage, freeing GPs for complex cases.
  - Ensure these teams work with shared records and care plans so patients aren’t shuffled between services. In areas where MDTs are functioning well, patients experience faster access and more consistent care.
  - Phased rollouts with clear milestones and local governance help keep quality and safety at the centre, even while changing how teams are configured.

- Safe staffing levels and meaningful appointment slots
  - Design workforce plans around safe staffing standards and realistic workloads, not just targets. Protect time for longer consultations for complex conditions and continuity where possible.
  - Maintain named clinicians for high-need patients to reduce repeated visits and miscommunication, which costs time and harms trust.

- Training, leadership and culture
  - Invest in the training pipeline, including return-to-practice, nurse associates and physician associates, with mentorship and supervision to ensure quality from the start.
  - Strong, supportive leadership and management that recognise workload pressures and empower front-line teams to innovate while keeping safety front and centre.

- Equity, digital access and patient involvement
  - Ensure rural and underserved communities aren’t left behind by addressing transport, digital access and language needs, so improvements are felt widely.
  - Engage staff and patients in co-designing changes, so the plan reflects real priorities and builds trust that reforms will endure.

In short, a workforce plan that prioritises transparent local data, robust modelling and clear evaluation tied to funding and planning will help us recruit and retain the right people, support safer, higher-quality care, and adapt as communities change. I’ve seen locally what works when teams are stable, supported and able to work at the right level of care for patients. If the plan keeps that focus, the NHS can deliver more timely, compassionate and reliable services for everyone that relies on them.

Any NHS workforce plan should prioritise targeted recruitment incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities—to attract and retain staff. This should include housing and transport support, local housing schemes and subsidised travel to make roles sustainable for those already living in the area or willing to relocate. Pairing these with practical career pathways and adequate funding for training helps build long-term resilience. 

For retention, the plan must enable flexible working: part-time roles, job-share, phased retirement, and varied shift patterns so staff can balance caring responsibilities, health, or long commutes. Access to affordable childcare and proactive mental health services is essential to prevent burnout and sustain morale. In our area, flexible scheduling and on-site wellbeing support have helped a few colleagues stay in posts they might otherwise leave. 

Additional measures like safe-staffing targets, supportive supervision, and rotational postings to share expertise between communities will maintain high-quality care. A workforce plan blending tangible incentives with real-life flexibility will better protect patients and staff alike and support timely access to services.

An NHS workforce plan must put people at the heart of care, balancing flexibility with safety and strong digital foundations. Key priorities should include flexible working options to recruit and retain a diverse workforce: part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and robust childcare support with predictable, well-staffed rosters to prevent burnout. In my experience, a local GP practice that introduced a two-day job-share and clearer shift patterns kept experienced staff and improved patient access. 

Staff wellbeing and development must be non-negotiable: protected time for mental wellbeing, confidential supervision, mentoring, and clear career progression pathways. Quick access to training and opportunities for skill mix across teams help staff feel valued and capable of delivering safe care. 

Interoperable, secure IT is essential: unified electronic records, secure systems, and staff digital training reduce admin burden and speed up referrals—while keeping safeguards for those who are digitally excluded by maintaining strong phone and in-person options.

Sensible workforce planning should also ensure safe staffing ratios, targeted recruitment (including international routes with proper support), and administrative capacity to let clinicians focus on patients. These priorities would help recruit, keep, and support staff while maintaining high-quality, timely care.

From my perspective in Wales, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise clear scope-of-practice, timely revalidation and robust indemnity, alongside targeted funding for protected clinical supervision to support new roles and safeguard patient safety. Clear definitions of who can do what, and under what supervision, reduce uncertainty for staff and patients and help teams work with confidence, especially in GP and community services where roles are expanding. Revalidation processes must be streamlined and adequately resourced so clinicians stay in practice rather than become bogged down by paperwork delays. Indemnity arrangements must be predictable, including for overseas-trained staff, to remove barriers to recruitment and to share accountability fairly. 

Crucially, fund protected supervision for roles such as advanced nurse practitioners, physician associates, and experienced practice nurses as they take on greater responsibility. Provide protected time for supervision, mentorship, and reflective practice, integrated with ongoing CPD and return-to-practice pathways. In my experience, when supervision is available and boundaries are well defined, staff feel safer, burnout falls, and patient safety improves. Let this be embedded within governance and quality frameworks across NHS Wales.

To ensure an NHS workforce plan that recruits, retains and supports staff while keeping high-quality, safe care, I would prioritise two interlinked strands. First, tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas (rural, urban deprivation, coastal): housing assistance near practices, subsidised transport, flexible rosters, and clear career progression. Our area has vacancies that persist where housing costs are high, leading to longer GP waits and stretched community teams. Without targeted incentives, staff will drift to towns with better living costs, harming access for the most deprived communities. Second, transparent localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. A single dashboard capturing vacancy rates, time-to-fill, staff turnover, training uptake, patient safety indicators and service backlogs would inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Local data should drive decisions about where to scale pilots and how to allocate money for admin and coordination time. Any expansion of multidisciplinary approaches must come with strong governance, GP oversight and links to bolstering GP capacity and community mental health teams, rather than defaulting to MDTs Obviously.... In short, invest in people where they’re needed most, and back it with precise, locally owned metrics and evaluations to prove impact.
